highlights.title: Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite far sooner than we thought
highlights.summary: Western intelligence officials worry that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit before the end of the year, suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought, German media reported Monday.
body: The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.

US lawmakers briefed on government intelligence first disclosed Russia's ambition to deploy a space-based nuclear weapon in early 2024. At the time, US officials said Russia had launched a test satellite in 2022 to test the effects of radiation on space hardware and pave the way for a future nuclear-armed craft, but that Russia had not yet sent a nuclear weapon into orbit.

highlights.title: GTA 6 Hacker Officially Walks Free After Judge's Final Warning
highlights.summary: The man responsible for one of the biggest Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks is finally out of prison, and the judge had one very simple message for him: Don't do it again, mister.
body: Arion Kurtaj, now 21, was released under supervision after being sentenced to seven years in prison for a series of cybercrimes committed as a teenager, according to the BBC. The hacker, a member of the notorious Lapsus$ gang, pleaded guilty to breaking into several major companies, including Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut.

Kurtaj pulled off the Rockstar breach in 2022 while staying at a Travelodge in Bicester, England — and while under police protection and on bail for other hacking offenses. With his computer confiscated, he reportedly used an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel's television, along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, to access Rockstar's internal systems.

He stole company data, including 90 clips showing nearly an hour of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6. He then broke into Rockstar's Slack messaging system and threatened to release the game's source code unless the company contacted him on Telegram. When Rockstar refused, Kurtaj published the stolen material online under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
points: The man responsible for one of the biggest Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks is finally out of prison, and the judge had one very simple message for him: Don't do it again, mister.

highlights.title: The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Plans to Blow Up Tons of Lead
highlights.summary: The US Army plans to blow up 9,500 pounds of lead azide held at an Iowa ammunition plant. Local officials say they learned most of the details through a press release.
body: On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.
“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

highlights.title: Activision calls Banjo-Kazooie one of its "iconic gaming franchises," raising hopes for long-awaited new game
highlights.summary: Banjo-Kazooie - the iconic Rare platformer starring an absent-minded bear and the sassy red bird he carries in a backpack - has been on hiatus for years, but a new Activision job listing has raised hopes for a new game.
body: In a LinkedIn post advertising a 'Product Manager, Emergent Franchises' role, the publisher wrote that it's "home to iconic gaming franchises including Call of Duty, Crash Bandicoot, Spyro the Dragon, and now… Halo, Age of Empires, Sea of Thieves, and Banjo Kazooie."

"Become part of the team working on building, growing, and shaping many of these franchises," the listing goes on. "As a Product Manager, you will serve as the publishing product lead for an upcoming premium console & PC title, driving the product from concept to launch."

If you're scratching your brain trying to remember when Activision took control of the beloved platformer, well, it happened during Xbox's last massive internal shakeup. Amid the mass layoffs and studio divestments, Xbox also made some drastic changes to its corporate structure - Halo, World's Edge and Rare were all slotted under Activision's supervision.

Rare's 40-year history includes almost too many notable games to list, but the internal rejig presumably put Activision in control of games like Conker, Viva Pinata and Killer Instinct, alongside the aforementioned pirate hit Sea of Thieves and Banjo-Kazooie.

highlights.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
highlights.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
body: Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

highlights.title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock
highlights.summary: Jensen Huang comes back, numbers go up. Maybe the reason behind the CEO’s return is just that simple?
body: The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value, until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the last month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia's board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back— with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

highlights.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
highlights.summary: Using agent teams and formal verification to improve quantum algorithms for fusion and chemistry.
body: Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support.

In a new paper, we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library, problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub.

Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover.
We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanity’s greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas.
points: Using agent teams and formal verification to improve quantum algorithms for fusion and chemistry.
Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers.
However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support.

body: Even though sleuthing fans were able to find it, the location is so secluded that Hanisch wondered if it would be feasible to get a crew of the necessary magnitude all the way up there. But once he saw the luscious greenery contrasting the jagged mountains, he knew they had found the arena for the Second Quarter Quell, and they’d have to make it work.

The next step was designing and building the Cornucopia — the focal point of the arena, which distinguishes each iteration of the Hunger Games (and each installment of the film franchise) from the others. Similar to the paradoxical landscape, Hanisch and his team wanted to create something that balanced beauty with danger. They landed on a blossom with metal spikes for petals, surrounded by thick beds of wildflowers, arranged by color, demarking each tribute’s position around the centerpiece.

“It’s very beautiful, it’s very elegant, but it also looks very deadly and evil,” Hanisch says. “When they were shooting the opening, and the tributes were all around with these capes, I thought this looked like one of those satanic, strange cults. I thought it was actually a very matching feel.”

body: Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.

For their part, politicians and the spokespeople of affected companies have denied such master plots. And while many presumed that the nationwide airline ground stoppage on 13 November resulted from the Federal Aviation Administration’s rollout of new AI-assisted administration software (called, perhaps aspirationally, the Smart System), the FAA themselves laid the blame on a downed router in Arkansas. Microsoft has chalked the recent outage to Outlook not to malicious intrusions, but some buggy code that has been laying dormant for months. Some people will buy such explanations. Others, naturally, may remain skeptical.
Just how worried should we be? Are these disruptions just a new, extremely annoying part of daily life?

The former Brazil forward brings a bit of glamour to the Cobblers and their Shoe Army will welcome that. But for Chris Hogg, in his first job as a manager, the day-to-day challenge of turning this struggling football club around continues - and it is hard work.

highlights.title: Should you give the statue to Benedict Halifax during 'Dubious Provenance' in GTA 6?
highlights.summary: Giving the statue to Halifax during the Grand Theft Auto 6 "Dubious Provenance" mission may not seem like the wisest choice, but don't be too quick to decide. In this GTA 6 mission, one choice is more rewarding and more time-efficient than the other.
body: Here's what happens if you give the statue to Benedict Halifax in GTA 6, as well as advice for dealing with him later on.

"Dubious Provenance" is one of the early main missions in Chapter 3. After Cal visits Boobie's apartment at the end of the "Dealer's Choice" mission, you will see a mission icon in the closet next to the kitchen. It's a pink symbol of a statue. Grab this statue to get the "visit the antique store" objective and start "Dubious Provenance."

The GTA 6 "Dubious Provenance" mission takes you to an antiques store in Capri, where Jason and Lucia try to sell the statue they found in Chapter 1. The owner won't have anything to do with the statue, but as you leave the store, a shady fellow named Benedict Halifax will run after you and offer to help. You're faced with a choice: give the statue to Halifax, or refuse.

Besides missing out on the watch and delaying the story, refusing to give Halifax the statue unlocks the opportunity to skip the quest (since calling Halifax is an optional objective). You probably shouldn't skip the quest, though, as you'll miss an entertaining storyline with plenty of loot at the end, including a standout vehicle.
